Thomas Manton
TOM-us MAN-tun
proper noun (figure)
English personal name. Thomas (Aramaic, "twin"); Manton, an English surname. Thomas Manton (1620-1677) was an English Puritan preacher and a clerk of the Westminster Assembly.

📖 Biblical Definition

Thomas Manton (1620-1677) was one of the great Puritan expository preachers, a clerk of the Westminster Assembly, and the author of vast bodies of sermon-commentary that Spurgeon and the Banner of Truth would later prize. Educated at Oxford, Manton ministered in Stoke Newington and then at St. Paul's, Covent Garden, in London. He was chosen as one of the clerks of the Westminster Assembly and was esteemed among the moderate Presbyterian Puritans. At the Restoration in 1660 he was offered the deanery of Rochester but, with some two thousand other ministers, was ejected from the Church of England by the Act of Uniformity (1662) for refusing to conform — one of the great body of ejected Puritans whose Nonconformity shaped English Dissent. Manton's enduring legacy is his preaching: his complete works run to twenty-two volumes, dominated by massive expository series, most famously his commentaries on James, Jude, and the 119th Psalm (the last running to 190 sermons). His preaching is plain, doctrinally rich, searching, and pastorally warm in the best Puritan manner. J.C. Ryle wrote the biographical introduction to Manton's collected works and ranked him among the soundest of the Puritan divines. Manton models the Puritan expository ideal: the patient, sequential, doctrinally-full preaching of the biblical text, applied searchingly to the conscience.

Great Puritan expository preacher (1620-1677); clerk of the Westminster Assembly; ejected in 1662 for Nonconformity; author of 22 volumes of sermon-commentary, including 190 sermons on Psalm 119; prized by Spurgeon and J.C. Ryle.

THOMAS MANTON, proper noun. English Puritan preacher (1620-1677).

Oxford-educated; ministered at Stoke Newington and St. Paul's, Covent Garden, London.

A clerk of the Westminster Assembly; among the moderate Presbyterian Puritans.

Ejected from the Church of England (1662) under the Act of Uniformity for Nonconformity.

Complete works in 22 volumes; famed expositions of James, Jude, and Psalm 119 (190 sermons). J.C. Ryle wrote his biographical introduction.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 119:11 — "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee."

James 1:22 — "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."

2 Timothy 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Nehemiah 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Thomas Manton is corrupted when his vast expository labor is dismissed as outdated Puritan verbosity, when his ejection is read as mere ecclesiastical politics rather than conscience-bound Nonconformity, or when the searching application that marks his preaching is lost in favor of mere information.

expand to see more

Verbosity dismissal. Twenty-two volumes, 190 sermons on a single psalm — modern readers, formed by brevity, may dismiss Manton's output as the long-windedness of a bygone age. The Puritan expository method was not padding but patience: the slow, sequential, doctrinally-full opening of the text, with searching application to the conscience at every turn. Manton's 190 sermons on Psalm 119 are not 190 ways of saying the same thing; they are 190 patient meditations that mine a single psalm for the whole of the Christian life. The reward of reading him is the reward of all the Puritans: depth that brevity cannot give.

Politics-not-conscience misreading. Manton's ejection in 1662, with some two thousand fellow ministers, is sometimes read as a casualty of Restoration church politics. For Manton it was a matter of conscience bound to Scripture: he would not subscribe what he could not affirm before God. The Great Ejection produced English Nonconformity and cost its ministers their livings, their pulpits, and often their liberty. Manton chose the loss rather than violate his conscience. The dictionary honors the conscience, not merely the historical event.
